title: The Room Between Entries
author: Lantern Original
summaryTr: Yıkım öncesi son inceleme için eski bir konaklama binasına giren Iona, annesinin tuttuğu tahliye kayıtlarında açıklanamayan boşluklar bulur. Binanın boş olduğunu onaylamadan önce, kayıtlarda yer almayan insanların seslerini anlaması gerekir.
paragraphs: The council had given Iona Vale a form with three boxes. The first asked whether the electricity had been disconnected. The second asked whether dangerous materials had been removed. The third asked whether all persons had left the premises. Beneath the boxes was a sentence in smaller print: The undersigned accepts responsibility for the accuracy of this declaration. Iona had signed hundreds of such forms. She had never previously considered how much weight the word all was expected to bear.

Morrow House stood behind the flood wall, a long brick building with windows too narrow for its broad, patient face. For thirty years it had provided temporary rooms for people who had nowhere else to go. After the flood, the council had closed it. Now a contractor wanted to demolish it before winter. Iona's mother had worked at its reception desk, and for that reason Iona should have refused the assignment. Instead, she had opened the folder and said she knew the building.

She arrived at four in the afternoon with Noor, a trainee surveyor whose yellow coat made the entrance look almost cheerful. The key turned reluctantly. Inside, the air smelled of wet wool and the powder used to clean old telephones. A man waited beside the reception desk, holding two paper cups. He introduced himself as Davi, the last porter. He had retired twelve years earlier, but apparently the council still had his number. He had brought coffee because the inspection would take longer than they thought.

Noor asked whether he had been there on the night of the flood. Davi looked at Iona before answering. 'I was on the other side of the river. Your mother sent me home early.' Iona took a cup she did not want. Her mother, Ruth Vale, had drowned while helping with the evacuation. That was the account in the newspaper and the account Iona had repeated whenever somebody asked. Her body had never been recovered. Neither fact was mentioned on the clearance form.

They began with the ground floor. Noor photographed the kitchen while Iona checked the service cupboards. Davi stayed close enough for his keys to be audible. In the dining room, fifty chairs stood on twenty tables. Their legs made a small forest against the ceiling. On one table someone had arranged a plate, a knife and a folded paper napkin. Iona touched the plate. It was warm. Davi put it into a cupboard without comment and closed the door with both hands.

At reception, Noor found a heavy register beneath a plastic sheet. The final page was dated twenty-one years earlier, the date of the flood. Most entries contained a room number, a name and a destination: sports hall, hospital, relative. Six entries had a straight line through the destination column. The last sentence read, All remaining residents transferred. Below it was Ruth Vale's signature. Iona recognised the unusual shape of the capital R, which resembled a woman turning to look over her shoulder.

'Don't copy that sentence,' Davi said. Noor's pencil stopped. 'Photographs are all right. Measurements are all right. But don't write that nobody's here.' He sounded embarrassed, as though giving instructions about a neighbour's difficult dog. Iona asked whether there were squatters. 'Sometimes there are people,' he replied. 'That isn't quite the same thing.' She told him that if he knew about unauthorised occupants, he had to say so. He looked at the three boxes on her form and said he was trying.

Upstairs, the first corridor contained twelve doors. The council plan showed twelve rooms. Noor numbered her photographs aloud, and Iona tested each handle. Room eight was locked. Room nine contained a bed frame and a wardrobe whose mirror faced the wall. Room ten was bare except for a damp rectangle where a picture had hung. When they reached the stairs, Noor said she had photographed thirteen doors. She showed Iona the images. Between nine and ten was a narrow green door with a brass number that had been polished beyond recognition.

They walked back. The green door was there. Iona measured the corridor, then measured the rooms on either side. The sums left no space for it. She tried the handle. From behind the door came the sound of someone dragging a suitcase across bare boards, followed by three polite knocks. Davi caught her wrist before she could knock in reply. 'Ask a question,' he whispered. 'Something the register couldn't answer.' Iona stared at him. He released her immediately, but the three knocks came again.

'What can you see?' she asked. A woman's voice answered, 'Room eleven, Miriam Saye, transferred to the sports hall.' Noor bent close to the brass plate. 'What can you see now?' Iona repeated. The woman said exactly the same words, with exactly the same breath between her name and her destination. There was no suitcase this time. Davi shook his head. 'Not her. Only what they wrote about her.' He led them downstairs before Iona could decide whether to be frightened or furious.

At the desk, he produced a biscuit tin containing letters, photographs and a notebook. He had tried to get the building examined before. Each time an inspection had ended early. Tools disappeared. Corridors changed. Once a contractor had been found outside, unable to remember the surname he had used for forty years. 'The house listens to the official account,' Davi said. 'When somebody tries to make it final, it corrects whatever doesn't fit.' Iona heard the careful tone of a person who had learned that speaking plainly made him less believable.

She called the council's duty officer. There was no signal, although her phone showed four bars. Noor offered hers and got the same result. Davi pointed to a red box beside the entrance: an old emergency telephone powered by a hand crank. It had connected to the flood station beyond the wall. A thick cable still ran from its back through the brickwork. 'That line doesn't go through reception,' he said. 'The others do.' Iona tried the front door. It opened onto the street. She could still leave.

That was the moment she would return to later, in the brief interval before sleep: the ordinary grey pavement, a delivery bicycle going past, the possibility of stepping out. Instead, she wanted an explanation that could survive daylight. She told Noor to record the discrepancies and wait near the entrance. Then she asked Davi to show her what he meant by the official account. He opened his notebook to a list of six names. Beside each name he had written things no council form would ask.

Leonie Price disliked pears because of their texture. Tomas Reed kept a broken radio because his daughter had given it to him. Safiya Bell counted staircases in sets of four. Iona recognised none of them. 'Those are the six without destinations,' Davi said. 'They were in the laundry corridor when the flood doors shut. Ruth thought the rescue team had taken them through the yard. The rescue team thought she'd moved them upstairs.' He rubbed the edge of the notebook. 'Nobody went back to look until the next day.'

Iona said her mother had gone back. It came out too sharply. Davi nodded. 'After she signed. After the officer told her the count was complete.' Outside, a bus sighed at the stop. The sound seemed unnecessarily distant. Davi had one letter from Ruth, written that evening and pushed under the porter's office door. It said: I have made them absent. I have to change it where I said it. Beneath that, in a hurried line: A name isn't enough. Tell someone who can answer you.

Noor called from the entrance. She was holding Iona's form against her clipboard. 'Which building number is this? Seventeen or nineteen?' Iona said seventeen. Noor looked down, made a short mark, then frowned. 'I didn't write that.' Across the third box, in Ruth Vale's unmistakable handwriting, were the words No persons remaining. The front door shut softly. Davi ran towards it. He pulled at the handle, but when it opened the dining room was on the other side, fifty upturned chairs and one warm plate.

Iona took the form. The paper was wet around the edges. She tore it across the third box, then into smaller pieces. The fragments fell onto the desk, where their fibres moved together like the legs of insects. A minute later the form lay whole beneath the register. Noor had gone very still. 'I only wrote the address,' she said. 'I know,' Iona answered. She made herself say it again. 'I know what you wrote.' Behind them, someone upstairs dragged a suitcase across bare boards.

The register now had a new line. Noor Awan, assistant inspector. In the destination column, a word appeared slowly, darkening from pale grey to black: transferred. Noor said that her hands felt cold. Iona reached for one, and for an instant could not remember whether the young woman had come with her or had been waiting inside. She said Noor's name aloud. The uncertainty passed. Davi opened his notebook. 'Tell me something about her. Something that happened today.' Iona described the yellow coat. 'Not what she is wearing. Something she did.'

That morning Noor had put a coin beneath a crooked café table. When the waiter offered to move them, she had said it would be crooked for the next customer too. Iona repeated the exchange, clinging to its unimportance. Davi wrote it down. Noor's fingers grew warmer. 'Now ask her about it,' he said. Iona asked why she had used a coin rather than folded paper. 'Paper goes soft when they wash the floor,' Noor replied. The word transferred faded, though it did not disappear.

For the first time, Davi looked hopeful. The house could repeat a record, he explained, but it could not carry on a conversation beyond what it held. The fragments behind the doors were statements wearing voices. Living people could answer, disagree, remember differently. The six residents had survived somewhere inside the building because he had continued writing to the council about them. Every unanswered letter had kept their disappearance unresolved. 'I thought I was achieving nothing,' he said. 'Perhaps nothing was what kept them alive.'

They needed someone outside to receive a correction. The red telephone was their only connection that the reception system did not control. Iona lifted its receiver while Davi turned the crank. There was a click, then a distant ringing. A woman answered, 'Flood station. State the number of persons awaiting transfer.' Her voice was Ruth's. Iona dropped the receiver so hard that it struck the wall. Davi checked the box and found the cable cleanly severed beneath it. The voice had come from an instrument connected to nothing.

The actual cable continued through a maintenance duct to the cellar, where its test terminal could be reached. Davi knew because he had repaired it during the building's last winter. They would need the crank unit and two lengths of wire. He fetched a screwdriver from his tin. Noor volunteered to read the six residents' names while they worked. At the third name she stopped. Her yellow sleeve had become the dull colour of the wall behind it. In the register, transferred was returning to black.

Iona asked about the coin again. Noor answered correctly, but her sleeve continued fading. They could not keep repeating the same memory. The house was learning their account as they spoke. Iona asked what Noor wanted for dinner. 'I want to go home,' she said angrily. 'I want you to stop testing whether I'm real.' The colour returned so abruptly that Iona flinched. She apologised. Noor was not a lock to be opened with the right question. She was afraid, and Iona had been treating her fear as a useful mechanism.

Getting the telephone apart took ten minutes. During that time they discussed ordinary things, badly. Davi confessed he had brought instant coffee in a flask because the café charged too much. Noor said she had known. Iona admitted she had taken this assignment to discover whether her mother had died courageously. 'Would you love her less if she hadn't?' Noor asked. Iona could not answer at once. The register rustled, but no new writing appeared. An honest hesitation, it seemed, was harder for the house to use than a confident lie.

They descended with the crank unit, the notebook and a torch. The cellar stairs were dry, yet each step made the sound of water being displaced. At the bottom, the walls carried a brown flood mark level with Iona's mouth. Davi pointed out the maintenance duct behind an iron grille. Its screws were deeply rusted. While he worked on them, Noor shone the torch along the passage. Six coats hung on hooks beside a closed fire door. Beneath them, on the clean concrete, six pairs of wet footprints waited without moving.

Then the footprints changed. One pair turned towards them. Behind the fire door, a man said, 'If you are taking names, mine is Tomas Reed.' Iona remembered the broken radio. Instead of asking about it, she asked what he had been doing before she arrived. 'Trying to make that woman stop humming,' he answered. Someone else said she would hum whatever she pleased. Noor gave a sudden, almost painful laugh. These voices interrupted one another. They were untidy and impatient. They belonged to people who did not know what answer was required.

The fire door had no handle on their side. Its inspection window was covered by a sheet of paper stating that the room had been cleared. Iona scraped away a corner with her thumbnail. Through the glass she saw a laundry trolley, a strip of fluorescent light and a woman sitting on an upturned bucket. The woman looked perhaps forty. In Davi's photograph, taken twenty-one years earlier, she had looked exactly the same. Behind her, the corridor extended farther than the building itself. Its far end was lost in a bright, depthless grey.

Davi spoke to the woman through the door. 'Leonie. It's Davi.' She stood so quickly the bucket rolled away. 'You said you'd bring blankets.' He closed his eyes. 'I know.' She asked how long they had been waiting. He told her. Silence followed, then a man began to swear. Iona had expected gratitude, recognition, relief. Instead, the people behind the door were furious with them. The sound steadied her. Whatever the house offered in exchange for obedience, it was unlikely to include the right to be inconvenient.

Noor asked whether Ruth Vale was with them. Leonie shook her head. Ruth had come to the window carrying the register. She had tried to cross out the final sentence, but the ink returned. A woman at reception had told her that one person could amend an address, but a completed transfer required acknowledgement at its destination. Ruth had gone to make a call. Later, water came under the door. 'We heard her in the passage,' Leonie said. 'Then we didn't.' She would not tell Iona anything kinder than what she knew.

While Davi worked, Tomas pushed a folded sheet beneath the laundry door. It was a list of people to contact, written on the back of a washing schedule. Several telephone numbers had too few digits. Iona recognised an address where a supermarket now stood. She could have pocketed the sheet and promised to make the calls, but Tomas was watching her through the cleared corner of glass. She told him that some addresses might have changed. He asked whether his daughter would still be at school. Iona said no.

He sat down where she could no longer see him. For a moment the only sound was Davi scraping rust from a screw. Then Tomas asked what happened to a parent who missed the whole of a child's growing up. Noor crouched beside the window. 'I don't know,' she said. 'But she may have spent those years thinking you chose to leave.' He moved close enough to the door that they could hear his breathing. 'I didn't,' he said. Noor wrote those two words beneath his daughter's old telephone number.

Leonie wanted to know whether they would be allowed to leave the hospital afterwards. The question startled Iona. Leonie explained that, before the flood, temporary accommodation had repeatedly turned into somewhere she needed permission to leave. She would not exchange this corridor for another locked door merely because the people on the other side used kinder voices. Iona could promise no hospital policy. She promised to record that Leonie had asked, and to stay until someone answered her directly. Behind her, the register's pages stirred as if irritated by the limits of that promise.

The two brothers asked for their bag to be passed out first. It caught beneath the door, and they began blaming one another. Iona almost told them to abandon it. Then she remembered that every object she herself had chosen to keep was waiting safely in an apartment outside. She and Noor worked the straps through one at a time. Inside were a chess set, three notebooks and a pair of shoes much too small for either brother. None of it explained their determination; none of it needed to. The bag finally slid free, and for the first time something had crossed the boundary intact.

Davi removed the grille. The cable terminal was intact, but the cupboard surrounding it had become a miniature reception desk. On its shelf lay a clean form. A woman stood in the passage behind them, wearing a grey cardigan with a council badge. Iona had not heard her approach. Her face was perfectly ordinary until one tried to remember it. 'We can correct the assistant's entry,' she said. 'An administrative error. Sign here, and the current inspection party may leave.' She placed a fountain pen beside the form.

The document named Iona, Noor and Davi. Beneath their names it declared the remainder of the premises unoccupied. Iona understood the bargain. They would get out by closing the question that had kept the six residents alive. She asked the woman her name. 'Duty registrar.' She asked whether the woman had a family. 'My responsibility is to maintain an accurate count.' Iona asked what happened when the count was wrong. The woman smiled. 'Then the circumstances must be brought into agreement with the count.'

Davi reached past the form to the cable. The registrar did not stop him. Instead, she spoke in his own voice: 'I was on the other side of the river.' Then Ruth's: 'Go home, Davi. I'll finish here.' His hand shook. Iona saw what the house was doing. It could not invent a future, but it could arrange the past until regret became unbearable. Davi had spent twenty-one years wishing he had stayed. The registrar offered him a different memory. In it, Ruth survived because he returned in time. He only had to sign.

'That wouldn't be what happened,' Davi said. The registrar replied that the distinction had caused him enough suffering. He set the crank unit on the floor and began stripping the wires with his pocketknife. Noor sat beside him to hold the torch. Iona stayed by the laundry door. She asked the six residents to describe themselves for the outside operator, and corrected her request when it sounded like another official interview. 'Tell us what you want somebody to know.' For a while nobody spoke. Then Safiya said she wanted her son to know she had waited for him.

A thin metallic note came from the telephone. Davi turned the crank again. This time a man answered, with traffic behind his voice. 'River maintenance control. Who is using the old emergency circuit?' Iona almost cried at the irritation in his question. She gave her name, her department and the building's address. The man said Morrow House was empty. She told him that it was not. He asked how many people were inside. The registrar moved closer, and the cellar seemed to narrow around that simple, reasonable question.

Iona started to say nine. Six residents, three inspectors. Then she saw Noor's clipboard lying at the foot of the stairs. Noor herself was no longer holding the torch. The light rested against Davi's knee, and where she had been sitting there was a pale, dry patch on the floor. The telephone operator repeated his question. From behind the laundry door, in a voice stripped of anger, Noor called Iona's name. Her entry had been completed while they concentrated on the others. She was now someone who had already been transferred.

Iona gave the operator all nine names, including her own, but refused to certify that there were only nine people. 'The number is not established,' she said. 'Keep the incident open. Read that back to me.' The registrar put one hand over the terminal. The line filled with a sound like pages being turned very quickly. Iona shouted, asking the operator to repeat the message. She heard only pieces: address, persons present, number not established. Then the noise stopped. The operator had acknowledged the correction. Somewhere above them, a door slammed open against the street.

The laundry door shuddered, but remained shut. Its paper notice had changed. Now it read: Transfer requires confirmation of receiving location. The operator was dispatching a fire crew. They would take several minutes. The registrar said the circuit could not be maintained that long. She was telling the truth. The crank unit was hot beneath Davi's hand, and the stripped wires had begun to smoke. Iona asked the operator to stay with them while Davi disconnected one wire. In the sudden silence, the house seemed to inhale.

They needed a destination that already existed, and someone there to confirm it. The street was a destination. The operator could not see it from his control room, but there was a camera on the flood wall. Iona remembered passing it. When Davi restored the connection, she told the operator to turn the camera towards the entrance. He said the old camera could not turn; it faced the service yard. Davi pointed to a low door at the end of the cellar passage. Beyond it was that same yard. They would have to open it from inside.

Iona ran towards the door. Halfway there, she heard her mother calling from an open office. Ruth sat behind a desk, younger than Iona was now, rubbing ink from her thumb. The sight brought back an ache so precise that Iona nearly stopped breathing. Her mother's bag stood on the floor. An orange lay beside it, scored around the skin with a thumbnail. Everything was right. Ruth looked up and said, 'I went back for them.' Iona wanted to kneel beside her. She wanted the story she had carried to be true in exactly the way she had imagined.

Instead, she asked, 'Did you know the door was closed when you signed?' Ruth looked down. 'All remaining residents transferred.' Iona asked again, and the sentence repeated. It was another fragment, assembled from a signature and a daughter's need. The registrar stood in the doorway beyond the desk. 'You can keep her as she was,' she said. Iona looked at the orange. Her mother always peeled oranges in one long strip, and often broke the strip halfway through. This one was perfect. It had no accidental history. She walked past it.

The yard door was held by two bolts. The lower one moved. The upper one had been painted into its socket, and Iona could not shift it. She called for help. For several seconds nobody came, and she understood how easily courage could become another flattering account told after an event. She was simply a frightened woman with insufficient strength. Then Davi arrived with the screwdriver. Together they chipped away the paint. Behind them, the telephone receiver lay on the floor, carrying the operator's increasingly urgent voice into the passage.

When the bolt released, cold evening air entered at ankle height. Davi pushed the door wide and ran into the yard. Iona could see the camera above the flood wall. Its small red light faced them. Davi waved both arms, then went back to the receiver, dragging the wire as far as it would reach. 'I'm in the service yard,' he said. 'I am Davi Mercer. I will receive whoever comes out. I am not confirming that the building is empty.' The distinction was his own, and Iona loved him for understanding it.

The paper over the laundry window split down the middle. Iona heard the handle on the other side turn. Leonie emerged first, blinking in the torchlight, followed by Tomas carrying a radio without its back panel. Safiya supported an older man whose left foot was wrapped in a towel. Two brothers came next, arguing over a bag they had both carried for what felt to them like an hour. Noor came last. She put her palm against Iona's cheek, not gently. 'Next time,' she said, 'we leave when the door is still a door.'

The registrar waited beside the stairs. Without moving, she seemed farther away each time Iona looked at her. 'A final total is required,' she said. Outside, Davi answered each person by name as the operator repeated it over the telephone. Iona told the registrar that a search team would establish what it could, and that uncertainty would remain in the report where evidence was missing. The woman looked almost bewildered. Her badge was now blank. Iona passed her and stepped into the yard without promising that nobody remained behind.

The fire crew arrived to find nine people under the camera, wrapped in blankets from an emergency locker. The six residents were taken to hospital. Their documents were old; their bodies were not. Reconciling those facts would occupy other departments for years. That night, Iona sat with Noor while Davi gave his statement. She did not ask Noor to forgive her. When Noor began to shake, she held the paper cup steady so she could drink. Beyond the wall, Morrow House had the dark, vacant appearance of any abandoned building.

Demolition was suspended. The report Iona eventually submitted included her mother's signature, Davi's unanswered letters and the names of officials who had accepted a completed count without checking the laundry corridor. It also included Iona's decision to remain after the first warning. Some colleagues advised her to remove that paragraph. She kept it. About Ruth, she wrote only what the witnesses could support: she signed an incorrect declaration, recognised the error and returned to attempt a correction. The search for her remains continued. Iona no longer needed uncertainty to look like disgrace.

Three months later, Noor returned to work in another department. Davi began visiting Leonie, who had discovered that she still disliked pears and now had twenty-one years of other dislikes to catch up on. The emergency circuit at Morrow House remained connected. No one was asked to certify an empty building. On the final page of the register, beneath the old sentence, Iona had written a new entry in her own ordinary handwriting: The previous declaration is withdrawn. Further information may be added. This account is not complete. She left enough space for another person's hand.

quiz.q: Why does Iona initially accept the inspection assignment?
options: She expects to recover valuable furniture.
She wants to understand her mother's final actions.
Noor insists on inspecting the building.
She plans to move the residents herself.
quiz.explainTr: Iona, annesinin ölümüne ilişkin anlatıyı ve son davranışlarını anlamak istediği için görevi alır.

quiz.q: What distinguishes the living residents from the voices copied by the house?
options: They can respond beyond the information in the records.
They never disagree with the inspectors.
They speak only when their names are read.
They remember every event outside the building.
quiz.explainTr: Yaşayan insanlar kayıtlı bilgilerin ötesinde cevap verebilir, karşı çıkabilir ve yeni konuşmalar geliştirebilir.

quiz.q: What has Davi's correspondence unintentionally achieved?
options: It has persuaded the council to repair the house.
It has destroyed the original evacuation register.
It has kept the residents' disappearance unresolved.
It has prevented time from passing outside.
quiz.explainTr: Cevapsız kalan mektuplar kaybolma olayının kesin biçimde kapanmasını engelleyerek içerideki insanların varlığını korumuştur.

quiz.q: Why does Iona refuse to certify that there are only nine people inside?
options: She cannot remember Davi's surname.
The operator forbids the use of numbers.
She wants to delay the fire crew.
A final total could exclude people who have not been found.
quiz.explainTr: Kesin bir toplam, henüz bulunmamış kişileri yok sayan yeni bir kapatma işlemine dönüşebilir; bu yüzden sayının belirlenmediğini söyler.

quiz.q: What does Iona's final report show about her changed attitude?
options: She accepts supported facts and uncertainty, including her own mistakes.
She decides all official records should be destroyed.
She proves her mother made no mistakes.
She considers a comforting account more useful than evidence.
quiz.explainTr: Iona annesini kusursuzlaştırmak yerine tanıklıkların desteklediği bilgileri, bilinmeyenleri ve kendi hatasını birlikte kayda geçirir.
